I have farmed this land in Quzhou for 35 years. I am 59 now, and I know every corner of my 13.1 mu. My household has four people — my husband and I do the farming, while my son and daughter-in-law work in a factory in Handan and send money home. Because their wages help with expenses, I do not need to chase the highest possible yields at any cost. I need a steady, reliable harvest that does not break my back or my budget.

My land is all wheat-maize rotation. I plant winter wheat in October on the full 13.1 mu, harvest it in early June, and immediately plant summer maize on the same 13.1 mu. That is the only system that makes sense here — the land gives us two crops a year, and I would never waste the growing season.

**For wheat:** I will buy improved wheat seed from the local supply store — not the old saved seed, because the new varieties resist disease better and the yield is more stable. Before sowing in mid-October, I will use rotary tillage to prepare the seedbed. I always apply basal compound fertilizer at sowing, then topdress with urea at green-up and jointing. I have a well, so I will irrigate four times: once before winter to protect the seedlings from freezing, once at jointing, once at heading, and once during grain filling if the weather turns dry. For chemicals, I spray herbicide once after sowing, and I usually need one or two sprays for insects or fungus — I watch the leaves and decide. I expect about 520 kg per mu if the spring weather cooperates.

**For maize:** Timing is everything after wheat harvest — I have maybe ten days to get the maize in the ground. I will buy hybrid maize seed, always hybrid, because the difference in yield is too big to ignore. I will plant no-till or with very light rotary tillage right after the wheat straw is cleared; there is no time for deep ploughing, and the soil is still loose from the wheat season. I apply fertilizer at planting and then topdress at the big trumpet stage when the plants are hungry. I irrigate three times: at jointing, big trumpet, and tasseling/silking. The maize needs less spraying than wheat — usually herbicide once and insecticide once or twice depending on the borers. I expect around 600 kg per mu.

I keep my inputs moderate. I have learned that throwing more fertilizer does not always mean more profit, especially with my son’s off-farm income reducing the pressure. But I will not cut corners on water — the well is my advantage, and irrigation is what saves the crop in a dry Hebei summer.
